paragraphs: Following a sound of interest requires the auditory system to organize incoming signals against distracting background sounds. This paper proposes a model of the early stages of that organization, addressing how auditory input becomes separated into streams. Its focus is the processing that can support selective listening.

The model connects current sound activity with traces left by earlier sounds. Incoming signals produce tonotopic patterns, meaning that activity is organized according to sound frequency. Traces of previous activity feed back into the system and influence how later signals are processed. Consequently, the interpretation of a sound depends partly on the recent history of stimulation.

The model's behavior agrees with several established psychophysical findings about auditory perception. This agreement supports the proposed interaction between present input and past activity as a possible mechanism for streaming. The contribution is a concrete account of how temporal context can shape perceptual grouping during the early processing of sound.
neurips-1995-a-model-of-auditory-streami.tldr: A model explains auditory streaming through feedback between frequency-organized sound activity and traces of earlier input.

paragraphs: The paper describes a neural classifier for reading the E13B characters printed along the bottom of checks. Recognition is divided between a hardware linear classifier and a second neural layer running in software on an inexpensive microprocessor. The software layer refines the hardware layer's output, giving the system two stages for reaching a character decision.

The hardware classifier is designed through mathematical constraints and an optimization objective. An active set method determines its weights, using an approach related to separating hyperplanes. The reported optimization solves for 1,523 Lagrange multipliers in 7.5 minutes on a SPARC 2, described as equivalent to training with approximately 128,000 examples.

The system also connects recognition with character positioning: a strong classifier response indicates that a character is horizontally centered. This integrates segmentation with recognition in a setting that includes noise and ink marks. On 1,500 real checks, the resulting network achieves 99.995% character accuracy. That figure describes individual character recognition, rather than the proportion of entire checks read without error.
neurips-1995-a-neural-network-classifier.tldr: A hardware classifier paired with a software neural layer reads check characters with a reported 99.995% character accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper presents a gesture recognition system that learns where to look while operating with an active camera in an unconstrained office. Existing vision routines locate salient body parts, and the camera is directed toward selected locations to acquire images of gestures or expressions. Camera targeting therefore becomes part of the recognition process.

The attention component uses reinforcement learning with hidden state and a multiple-model formulation of Q-learning. Its objective is successful recognition, so the usefulness of a viewing target is tied to how well it helps distinguish a gesture. This links the system's visual actions to the particular recognition problem it is trying to solve.

Given target gestures and distracting alternatives, the system can learn which locations provide the strongest discrimination for a particular gesture. The stated finding shows that visual attention can be learned through the recognition objective itself. It makes the choice of what to inspect an adaptable component of the system, alongside the processing of the resulting images.
neurips-1995-active-gesture-recognition-.tldr: An active-camera gesture recognizer uses reinforcement learning to choose viewing targets that best distinguish gestures.

paragraphs: The paper develops a classifier training method aimed directly at reducing misclassification. During learning, examples receive probabilistic class assignments. These distributions must balance expected classification error, the required structure of the classifier, and a controlled amount of randomness measured by Shannon entropy.

The authors express this constrained problem through a free-energy objective and extend deterministic annealing to enforce structural requirements. A temperature parameter governs the progression of learning: as temperature falls, assignment entropy and expected cost are reduced. At low temperature, assignments become hard class decisions, and the procedure directly targets error while producing the required classifier structure.

This formulation matters because it connects the classification objective with constraints on how the classifier can be built. The framework accommodates multiple structures, and the reported comparisons concern radial basis function design. Across several benchmarks, it substantially outperforms other design methods, often with computational design complexity comparable to, or only moderately above, methods based strictly on descent. The reported benefit therefore combines improved classification with a manageable optimization burden.
neurips-1995-an-information-theoretic-le.tldr: A constrained annealing algorithm turns probabilistic assignments into structured classifiers while directly targeting classification error.

paragraphs: The paper adds context-dependent phone classes to a speech recognizer combining a neural network with a hidden Markov model. Phones are the speech sound units being classified. The approach allows their probability estimates to reflect context, extending a system whose neural predictions originally treated phone classes independently of that context.

The design is modular. Separate single-layer networks distinguish among context classes using both the phone class and acoustic observations. Their outputs are combined with those of a context-independent network to produce context-dependent phone probabilities. This gives the original phone model and the additional context models distinct responsibilities within the recognizer.

Experiments report average word error reductions of 16% on the ARPA 5,000-word task and 13% on the SQALE 20,000-word task, relative to the context-independent system. Decoding also becomes more than twice as fast, which the abstract attributes to improved modeling. The findings show that adding context through this modular construction improves both recognition accuracy and the speed of obtaining a transcription.
neurips-1995-context-dependent-classes-i.tldr: Modular context networks improve a hybrid speech recognizer's word error rates and more than double its decoding speed.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to estimate Bayes risk from labeled examples in a classification problem with multiple classes. Bayes risk describes the best achievable expected classification loss when the underlying probabilities are known. Estimating it helps characterize the difficulty of the classification problem itself, beyond the performance of any particular trained classifier.

The proposed method uses nearest neighbors in the sample data. It does not require the class-conditional probability distributions or the prior probabilities of the classes to be supplied. That makes the method applicable when researchers have classified observations but lack an explicit probabilistic description of how those observations were generated.

The approach does assume that sufficiently smooth class-conditional distributions accurately describe the problem. Its ability to work without known probabilities therefore rests on a regularity assumption about those unknown distributions. The paper illustrates the method on two pattern recognition problems. Its central contribution is a sample-based route to estimating an underlying performance limit under that stated smoothness condition.
neurips-1995-estimating-the-bayes-risk-f.tldr: A nearest-neighbor method estimates multiclass Bayes risk from labeled data without requiring known class distributions or priors.

paragraphs: The paper develops an approximation for inference and learning in probabilistic neural networks whose full computations are difficult. Its starting point is that a complicated network can contain substantial internal structures that remain computationally manageable. Those structures provide information that an approximation can preserve and use.

The proposed mean field framework avoids treating every unit as an independent degree of freedom. Instead, it incorporates large tractable substructures into the approximation. This matters because assuming complete independence discards relationships even when those relationships could be handled efficiently. The refined approach directs approximation toward the parts responsible for the computational difficulty.

The authors illustrate the framework with a first-order hidden Markov model extended by weak higher-order interactions. The first-order structure remains intact, while mean field theory handles the additional corrections. This example makes the division of labor concrete: retain the manageable dependence structure and approximate the extra interactions. The contribution is a principled way to build an approximation around what can already be computed effectively.
neurips-1995-exploiting-tractable-substr.tldr: A refined mean field method preserves tractable network dependencies while approximating the interactions that make computation difficult.

paragraphs: Neural networks can learn useful decision rules that are difficult for people to understand. This paper introduces TREPAN, an algorithm that turns the behavior of a trained network into a symbolic decision tree. The goal is to give people a comprehensible representation of the concept the network has learned.

TREPAN uses queries to construct a tree that approximates the network. The trained network supplies the behavior to be represented, while the tree provides an explicit structure for expressing decisions. This creates two relevant standards of success: the tree should agree with its source network and should remain accurate as a predictor in its own right.

The experiments report trees that combine strong agreement with their networks, comprehensibility, and predictive accuracy. The authors also report broad applicability and good scaling to large networks and high-dimensional inputs. These findings support extracting a readable model after neural training. The result is an approximation of the learned concept, with fidelity to the original network serving as a central measure of its usefulness.
neurips-1995-extracting-tree-structured-.tldr: TREPAN queries trained neural networks to construct readable decision trees that closely reproduce their predictions.

paragraphs: The paper presents a learning framework for hidden Markov models with distributed hidden states. A distributed representation describes a state through multiple components, so learning must account for combinations of those components. This representation makes the hidden-state calculation combinatorial and creates a central computational challenge.

The authors derive a maximum-likelihood learning algorithm using expectation-maximization. Its maximization step has an exact analytical solution, analogous to the familiar updates for a standard hidden Markov model. The expectation step, however, becomes intractable because it must deal with the combinations in the hidden representation. The difficulty is therefore concentrated in a specific part of the learning procedure.

To make that step manageable, the paper derives a simple mean field approximation. Experiments suggest that both this approximation and Gibbs sampling provide viable alternatives to the expensive exact algorithm. The contribution combines a learning formulation with practical ways to handle its bottleneck, making distributed hidden-state models accessible without requiring exact computation throughout the entire training process.
neurips-1995-factorial-hidden-markov-mod.tldr: Factorial hidden Markov models use distributed hidden states and approximate inference to make their otherwise intractable learning procedure practical.

paragraphs: The paper presents a face detector that applies a neural network to small image windows. Each window receives a decision about whether it contains a face. The system also arbitrates among multiple networks, combining their decisions to improve performance beyond what a single network achieves.

A central training problem is choosing examples of images that are not faces. Such images cover an enormous variety of possible appearances, making manual selection difficult. The authors use a bootstrap process that adds false detections to the training set as learning proceeds. The detector's own mistakes therefore identify non-face examples that need further attention during training.

This creates a direct connection between observed errors and the construction of the training data. The paper reports comparisons with another leading face detection system and finds better performance in both detection and false-positive rates. Together, the results support a system combining local neural classification, decisions from multiple networks, and repeated training on the misleading image regions the detector actually encounters.
neurips-1995-human-face-detection-in-vis.tldr: A neural face detector combines multiple networks and learns from its false detections to improve detection and false-positive rates.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how to make a committee of neural networks more useful than its individual members. Its central concern is the relationship between their errors. If members tend to make mistakes on the same cases, combining them has less opportunity to improve performance. The authors therefore focus on encouraging independence among those errors.

Their approach trains the networks on different resampled versions of the original training set. Changing which examples each member learns from offers a way to influence the similarities between the resulting networks. The question is whether differences introduced through training data can produce the error diversity that a successful committee needs.

The methods are tested on an artificial sinwave task and on hepatoma and breast cancer diagnosis problems. This places the investigation in both an artificial setting and practical diagnostic applications. The abstract describes the methods and testing scope without stating a measured improvement. The contribution is the investigation of resampling as a way to control committee error relationships, a property that individual network accuracy alone does not capture.
neurips-1995-improving-committee-diagnos.tldr: The paper studies whether training networks on different resampled datasets can reduce shared errors in diagnostic committees.

paragraphs: This paper applies reinforcement learning to elevator dispatching, a control problem with changing demand and incomplete information. Elevator operation unfolds in continuous time with discrete events and a continuous state space. Passenger arrival rates also change, so the learning system must act in a setting whose behavior is not stationary.

The system uses a team of agents, each controlling one elevator car. All agents receive a shared reinforcement signal describing the team's performance. For any individual agent, that feedback appears noisy because it also reflects other cars' actions, random passenger arrivals, and aspects of the state the agent cannot observe. Learning must therefore connect local decisions with a shared outcome.

Despite these complications, the reported simulation results exceed those of the best heuristic elevator controllers known to the authors. The result supports reinforcement learning for a large stochastic control problem with interacting decision makers. Its stated scope is simulation, where the approach succeeds despite combining partial observability, changing demand, and team-level feedback.
neurips-1995-improving-elevator-performa.tldr: A team of reinforcement learning agents controls elevator cars and outperforms the authors' strongest known heuristic controllers in simulation.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a learner can acquire assumptions that suit a particular domain. Such assumptions constitute model bias: they guide which explanations or predictors the learner considers appropriate. The proposed route is to learn many related tasks from that domain, allowing their common structure to inform the learning process.

The theoretical contribution bounds how many tasks must be learned to acquire an appropriate bias. A consequence concerns tasks known to share an internal representation or preprocessing step. Under that assumption, learning tasks together reduces the examples needed per task by distributing the burden of learning shared structure across the collection. The result separates task-specific requirements from the additional requirements associated with learning independently.

An experiment provides strong qualitative support for the theory. The stated significance is that related tasks can help establish how a domain should be represented, and that shared representation can improve generalization efficiency. The common-representation assumption is central to the sample-requirement result: the benefit comes from structure that the tasks can actually share.
neurips-1995-learning-model-bias-cc866e0.tldr: Learning related tasks together can acquire a useful domain bias and reduce per-task data requirements when the tasks share a representation.

paragraphs: The paper models how the visual system chooses targets for saccades, the rapid eye movements that bring interesting locations onto the fovea. These movements are ballistic: the muscle activation pattern is determined before movement, without visual feedback during it. Target selection must therefore provide a location in advance of the movement.

The proposed model represents a scene using oriented spatial filters at multiple scales. Its search moves from coarse information toward finer detail, comparing responses from the largest-scale filters first. This gives the targeting strategy an organized way to use broad scene structure before examining smaller visual features.

The authors compare the model's predictions with eye movements recorded from people performing a natural visual search task. Preliminary results show substantial agreement between predicted and observed movements. This supports the proposed combination of multiscale representations and coarse-to-fine search as an account of targeting behavior. The evidence is explicitly preliminary, but it connects a computational search strategy to measured human decisions about where to look next.
neurips-1995-modeling-saccadic-targeting.tldr: A coarse-to-fine model using multiscale visual filters predicts eye-movement targets with preliminary agreement to human search behavior.

paragraphs: This paper studies the expressive capacity of neural networks through VC dimension. This measure concerns how flexibly a model class can assign labels to examples and is relevant to reasoning about generalization. The question is how that capacity grows with the number of network weights and how activation functions affect the answer.

The authors establish a quadratic lower bound in the number of weights for networks using continuous activation functions. In other words, the capacity considered can grow at least as fast as the square of the weight count. This resolves whether the established O(w log w) bound for hard-threshold networks also extends to more general sigmoidal networks.

The result shows that the hard-threshold bound cannot simply be carried over to the more general setting. Counting weights alone therefore needs to be interpreted alongside the kind of activation used. The paper discusses consequences for the number of samples needed to support valid generalization. Its contribution is a theoretical capacity distinction with implications for sample requirements, rather than an empirical comparison of training procedures.
neurips-1995-neural-networks-with-quadra.tldr: A quadratic VC-dimension lower bound shows that the capacity bound for hard-threshold networks does not extend to general sigmoidal networks.

paragraphs: A linear threshold element makes a decision from the sign of a weighted sum of its inputs. Although this rule is simple, representing some functions can require very large integer weights. The paper studies the minimum weight sizes needed for such representations, motivated by the practical difficulty of implementing large weights.

Earlier distinctions separated functions requiring polynomial-size weights from those requiring exponential-size weights. The authors refine the polynomial side of that division, proving that it contains distinct subclasses according to the degree of the polynomial. Thus, functions whose weights are all described as polynomially bounded can still differ meaningfully in their minimum requirements.

The paper also states a more general existence result for minimal-weight threshold functions across input counts and weight sizes. Its proofs use a new technique for constructing functions with minimal weights. The contribution is a finer description of representational demands: knowing that a function admits polynomial-size weights does not fully characterize how large those weights must be to implement it.
neurips-1995-on-neural-networks-with-min.tldr: The paper proves a finer hierarchy of threshold functions based on the minimum integer weight sizes needed to represent them.

paragraphs: The paper formulates asset allocation as a Markov decision problem, treating investment choices as a sequence of decisions. This makes the problem accessible to dynamic programming and reinforcement learning. The aim is to optimize an allocation strategy within that sequential framework, linking current choices to the value of subsequent decisions.

The authors first use an artificial exchange rate to compare the approaches. In this setting, the policy learned through Q-learning is shown to be equivalent to one computed using dynamic programming. This provides a concrete connection between a learned strategy and a policy obtained through the dynamic programming formulation.

The approach is then tested on investing liquid capital in the German stock market. Neural networks approximate the value function, enabling the method to work with a high-dimensional state space. The resulting strategy outperforms a heuristic benchmark policy in the reported test. Together, the two applications support the feasibility of the formulation and the use of neural value approximation for a more complex allocation problem.
neurips-1995-optimal-asset-allocation-us.tldr: A sequential asset-allocation method matches dynamic programming in an artificial setting and beats a heuristic benchmark in a stock-market test.

paragraphs: The paper investigates a visual response pattern shared across different biological systems: a receptive field whose center and surrounding region have opposing effects. The authors show that analogous patterns emerge in an artificial neural network trained to locate edges in luminance. This connects a biological response structure with the demands of a specific visual task.

When background noise increases relative to the signal, the artificial network's hidden-unit receptive fields become broader and shallower. The authors also experimentally observe this kind of adjustment in bipolar cells of the carp retina. They connect it with previously described behavior in cells of the fly's compound eye, showing a parallel across structurally different visual systems.

Related changes also appear in the systems' two-phase responses to flashes, extending the comparison from spatial filtering to temporal filtering. The findings suggest that these response properties adapt to support detection of changes in space and time. The shared behavior of learned artificial units and biological neurons supports a functional explanation for both the receptive-field shape and its sensitivity to noise.
neurips-1995-plasticity-of-center-surrou.tldr: Artificial and biological visual systems show similar noise-dependent changes in their spatial and temporal responses.

paragraphs: The paper explores how a robotic hand can learn basic manipulation behaviors through sensory experience. Its motivation comes from infant exploration, where practiced sensorimotor patterns become components of more complex actions. The system uses an embodied lightweight hand intended for a humanoid, giving the learning process a physical manipulation setting.

A neural reinforcement learning algorithm learns primitive grasping procedures from sensory inputs. Two additional modules prepare sensory information for this process. One uses competitive learning to recognize object hardness, while the other uses backpropagation to detect shear. The architecture therefore connects learned sensory interpretation with learning how to act.

The reported system learns consistently and quickly during its initial training and remains adaptable to new situations afterward. This matters because the primitive behaviors are intended to function as reusable components of more elaborate actions. The contribution demonstrates an approach in which grasp learning and sensory preprocessing work together, with continued adaptability forming part of the stated outcome rather than learning ending permanently after initial training.
neurips-1995-primitive-manipulation-lear.tldr: A robotic hand combines reinforcement learning with learned sensory preprocessing to acquire adaptable grasping behaviors.

paragraphs: This paper develops recursive estimation algorithms for dynamic models built from multiple Gaussian radial basis function networks. A gating mechanism determines how the component networks participate. The authors consider two forms of gating: a scalar that changes with time and a state-dependent mechanism resembling a mixture of local experts.

The estimation procedure uses Kalman filtering both for the component models and for the gating probabilities. Learning therefore includes two connected tasks: adjusting the models and estimating which model is appropriate. Considering both time-varying and state-dependent gating gives the framework different ways to express changes in the relevance of its components.

The paper develops hard and soft competition variants. Under hard competition, only the network judged most probable is adapted. Under soft competition, every network is updated, with data weighted according to its responsibility. This distinction determines how learning experience is distributed among the components. The contribution is a set of recursive algorithms that jointly address model adaptation and the changing allocation of data to local models.
neurips-1995-recursive-estimation-of-dyn.tldr: Kalman-filter-based algorithms jointly adapt modular RBF models and their gating probabilities using hard or weighted competition.

paragraphs: The paper describes specialized, low-power analog-to-digital converters intended for speech and music processing. Their distinguishing feature is that analog circuits model aspects of biological hearing before the signal is converted to digital form. Auditory processing is therefore built into the acquisition hardware itself.

The authors present a converter design and a working system assembled from several copies of the chip. Together, these chips compute multiple representations of the same analog sound input. The use of several representations is central to the system: the hardware produces different processed descriptions of sound that support an auditory scene analysis approach.

The stated finding is a demonstration that such an approach can plausibly be implemented inexpensively. The working system connects biologically inspired sound processing with a concrete hardware realization, while the low-power converter design addresses the practical form that realization can take. Its significance lies in showing how auditory representations can be produced during signal conversion, making the front end an active part of sound analysis.
neurips-1995-silicon-models-for-auditory.tldr: Low-power converter chips use analog models of hearing to produce multiple sound representations before digital processing.

paragraphs: The paper presents SPERT-II, a hardware system developed for neural network computation and other signal processing applications. The authors design and implement a vector microprocessor, then package it as an attached processor for a conventional workstation. The workstation can thus use an additional processor built for these computational workloads.

The evaluation focuses on neural network training with backpropagation. Performance is compared with commercial workstations running code that has received extensive manual optimization. This comparison matters because the reported advantage is measured against implementations whose software performance has already been carefully improved, giving the hardware result a demanding reference point.

SPERT-II delivers significant speedups in those training comparisons. The abstract presents the contribution as a completed processor and system implementation with demonstrated performance benefits. Its significance is the connection between processor design and the computational demands of neural training: an attached vector processor can substantially accelerate the evaluated backpropagation work while remaining part of a conventional workstation-based computing setup.
neurips-1995-spert-ii-a-vector-microproc.tldr: SPERT-II is an attached vector processor that significantly accelerates backpropagation training relative to heavily optimized workstation implementations.

paragraphs: This paper develops a statistical account of overtraining and asks how much early stopping improves generalization. The analysis concerns realizable stochastic neural networks trained with Kullback-Leibler loss. These conditions define the setting of the theoretical conclusions, including the assumption that the learning model can represent the process being learned.

In the asymptotic regime, the authors find only a small generalization benefit from early stopping, even when the best stopping time is available. They also analyze stopping based on cross-validation and address how examples should be divided between training and testing to obtain optimal performance. This connects the stopping decision with the cost of reserving data to make it.

The paper reports a different conclusion in the non-asymptotic region: cross-validated early stopping decreases generalization error within the studied setting. Large-scale simulations agree closely with the analytical findings. The main lesson is that the benefit of early stopping depends on the statistical regime, and that evaluating cross-validation requires considering both its stopping guidance and the allocation of examples.
neurips-1995-statistical-theory-of-overt.tldr: A statistical analysis finds small asymptotic gains from early stopping but benefits from cross-validated stopping in the studied non-asymptotic regime.

paragraphs: The paper examines stochastic hillclimbing as a reference method for evaluating genetic algorithms on combinatorial optimization problems. The central question is whether relatively simple search methods can match the performance attributed to genetic algorithms. The authors investigate two problems already addressed by genetic algorithms: Koza's multiplexer problem and jobshop scheduling.

On these problems, the stochastic hillclimbing methods achieve results comparable to or better than the genetic algorithms designed for them. This makes the baseline consequential: a successful genetic algorithm needs to be assessed against an effective simpler search procedure. The reported findings concern these two problem settings and their corresponding algorithms.

The jobshop analysis also shows that constructing a hillclimbing method can reveal ways to improve the encoding used by a genetic algorithm. The comparison therefore contributes both an evaluation standard and insight into representation design. Its broader methodological point is that a baseline can help explain performance and improve the method being evaluated, rather than serving only as a score to exceed.
neurips-1995-stochastic-hillclimbing-as-.tldr: Simple stochastic hillclimbing matches or beats genetic algorithms on two studied problems and helps improve a jobshop encoding.

paragraphs: The paper addresses pneumonia risk assessment in a setting where medical decisions unfold sequentially. A clinician must judge risk using currently available information, while additional tests may become available later. Ordering every potentially useful test immediately is too expensive, so prediction must work before the full clinical record exists.

The authors introduce two complementary methods. Rankprop improves how a backpropagation network orders patients by risk compared with training using squared error. Multitask learning draws on later laboratory tests recorded in the training data, even though those results are unavailable when the deployed system must make its prediction. Later information thus contributes to learning without becoming a required input at prediction time.

Together, the methods improve the reported accuracy of neural networks on the pneumonia risk problem by 10–50%. The findings connect two aspects of the application: the importance of prioritizing patients correctly and the opportunity to learn from richer historical records. The authors describe both methods as broadly applicable, with the reported evidence coming from this risk-assessment task.
neurips-1995-using-the-future-to-sort-ou.tldr: Rankprop and multitask learning improve pneumonia risk assessment by refining patient ranking and learning from later tests available only during training.
